clue.text: Conceptually, they think timeless portholes must be scrapped aboard ship at sea

indicators.note: being aboard a vessel means being inside it, so one set of letters goes within the other
something at sea is confused and adrift, so the letters of ship are jumbled
scrapping portholes breaks them up, so their remaining letters are rearranged
being without time means losing T, the standard abbreviation for time, from the word

explanation.surface: A shipwright orders the portholes on a vessel at sea to be scrapped.
explanation.walkthrough: Two anagram signals are at work: 'scrapped' for the porthole letters and 'at sea' for the ship, with 'aboard' putting the first jumble inside the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Philosophers are thinkers who deal in abstract ideas, so they think conceptually.

clue.text: Drop producer's best sci-fi films back-to-back

parts.note: to pip is to beat narrowly, to best
two copies of the sci-fi film E.T. placed back to back, the second one facing the other way

explanation.surface: A boast that a producer's top science-fiction films ran in a double bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back-to-back' sets ET against its own mirror image, giving ETTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipette is a laboratory tube used to dispense liquid one drop at a time, so it produces drops.

clue.text: Contents of yellower organic compound

indicators.note: the contents of a word are everything inside its outer letters

parts.note: yellow means cowardly, so yellower is TIMIDER

explanation.surface: A chemist describes what is inside a more yellow organic substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yellower' is not to be taken literally: it is the comparative of yellow meaning cowardly, TIMIDER, whose insides are the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An imide is a chemical compound containing the group CONHCO, part of organic chemistry.

clue.text: Think too much about delivering eggs purchase

indicators.note: delivering words means speaking them, so these words are judged by their sound

parts.note: ova is the biological term for eggs; a purchase is leverage, which lets you prise something open

explanation.surface: Someone frets too much over a shopping trip to buy eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, OVA PRISE sounds like OVERPRIZE; purchase here is grip or leverage, not buying.
explanation.definitionFit: To overprize something is to value it too highly, giving it more thought and worth than it deserves.

clue.text: Poet and his sex-fuelled overdose

indicators.note: the overdose is filled up with fuel, so the other letters go inside it

parts.note: in the poet's own Latin, sex means six, which is VI in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A racy tale about a poet and a lustful overdose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sex' is Latin for six, the language of the Roman poet himself, hence 'his'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovid was a Roman writer of verse, author of the Metamorphoses and the Art of Love.

clue.text: Hunter having long how-d'ye-do in Wells?

indicators.note: the yearning and fuss are placed inside the writer's initials

parts.note: H.G. Wells, the science-fiction writer, gives his initials HG
to long for is to yen, have a yearning
a how-d'ye-do is a fuss or commotion, an ado

explanation.surface: A hunter strikes up a lengthy greeting in the town of Wells.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wells' looks like the cathedral city in Somerset, but it is the author H.G. Wells, giving his initials.
explanation.definitionFit: The hyena dog, or African wild dog, is a pack predator that chases down antelope.

clue.text: Ex-CE guru

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ... Sunak, a former Chancellor of the Exchequer
second meaning: a Hindu sage or holy teacher

explanation.walkthrough: CE abbreviates Chancellor of the Exchequer, Britain's finance minister; Rishi Sunak held that post before becoming Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the given name of a former UK finance minister and the Sanskrit title for an inspired sage.

clue.text: West African's takeaway battered eels

definitions.note: read as 'West African is'; the answer is a noun for a person from Togo

parts.note: food bought 'to go' is a takeaway

indicators.note: battered means beaten about, so the letters of eels are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A West African's takeaway meal is eels fried in batter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battered' suggests fish-shop cooking, but it rearranges EELS into LESE.
explanation.definitionFit: A Togolese is a native of Togo, a country on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa.

clue.text: Film director improves boxing movie's trailer

indicators.note: boxing something means enclosing it, so the last letter goes inside

parts.note: mends means repairs or improves

indicators.note: the trailer of a word is what trails at its end, its last letter

parts.note: the word movie, whose last letter is E

explanation.surface: A film director polishes the trailer for a boxing picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxing movie' suggests a fight film; boxing is the container and trailer the final letter of movie.
explanation.definitionFit: Sam Mendes is the English director of American Beauty, Skyfall and 1917.

clue.text: Purse tiny child pinched by middle of week's peak viewing

parts.note: to prim is to purse the lips primly

indicators.note: being pinched by something means being held tightly inside it
the middle of a four-letter word is its two central letters

parts.note: the word week, whose two central letters are EE
Tiny Tim is the small child in Dickens's A Christmas Carol

explanation.surface: A tiny child's purse is stolen midweek during the best television hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purse' looks like a noun for a wallet, but it is the verb, as in pursing the lips.
explanation.definitionFit: Prime time is the evening slot when the largest television audiences watch.

clue.text: Lower half of 25 I brutally punish

parts.note: 25-down is PSST; as a down entry its lower half is its last two letters
I as the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A threat to inflict harsh punishment with only half a grid reference.
explanation.walkthrough: The 25 points to 25-down, PSST; in a down light the lower half is the end, ST.
explanation.definitionFit: To stone someone is to pelt them with rocks, a savage form of punishment or execution.

clue.text: Peerless rider clobbering Southern luvvies

indicators.note: clobber is slang for clothes, so clobbering means dressing round, putting the S inside

parts.note: THE, stressed, means the one and only, without peer
a rider is an addition, like PS, a postscript

explanation.surface: A champion jockey beats up a crowd of southern theatricals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobbering' looks like violence but here means clothing, from clobber for clothes. Luvvies is British slang for actors.
explanation.definitionFit: Thesps, short for thespians, are actors, mocked in Britain as luvvies for their gushing manner.

clue.text: One of a pair used to clean plant

definitions.text: One of a pair used to clean
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a British brand of rubber washing-up gloves
second meaning: a yellow or orange garden flower

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, Marigolds are the familiar yellow rubber gloves worn for cleaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The name covers both a brand of household rubber glove and a bright orange flowering annual.

clue.text: Outlandish 8-point letter about hearing aid?

parts.note: X scores 8 points in Scrabble; the letter's name is spelt EX
otic means relating to the ear, the business of a hearing aid

explanation.surface: An odd letter of complaint about a hearing aid.
explanation.walkthrough: The 8 points are a Scrabble score: the X tile is worth 8.
explanation.definitionFit: Exotic means strange and foreign, just as outlandish describes something bizarre or alien.

clue.text: Population's not up, up or up to you?

indicators.note: not marks letters that must be left out of the jumble
up means stirred or in disorder, so the remaining letters are mixed

parts.note: the word population, with 's read as 'is'
the letters U and P are the ones taken out

explanation.surface: A question about whether a falling population is a matter of choice.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove U and P from POPULATION and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something optional is left to your choice, not compulsory.

clue.text: She's not common but would be if she gained a pound

definitions.text: She's not common but would be if she gained a pound

parts.words: She's not common but would be if she gained a pound
parts.note: a noblewoman is no commoner, but adding L, the pound sign, to her title makes a word meaning numberless, which is common in another sense

explanation.walkthrough: Pound is L; put it into the answer and you get COUNTLESS, which is very common indeed.
explanation.definitionFit: A countess is the wife of an earl or count, a titled aristocrat and so no commoner.

clue.text: Old Jordanian ate nuts with banana

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so these letters go mad and are reordered

explanation.surface: An ancient Jordanian dined on nuts with a banana.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like part of the menu, but it shuffles ATE and BANANA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nabataeans were an ancient Arab people whose capital Petra lies in modern Jordan.

clue.text: One of a host perhaps unfairly laid off day earlier

indicators.note: coming earlier puts the day's letter at the front
something done unfairly is done wrongly, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A worker unfairly made redundant the day before.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth saw 'a host of golden daffodils', which explains the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth's poem describes a crowd of these yellow spring flowers, so the answer is an example of one of that host.

clue.text: Ahead starting off 9th, then all square, with Koepka finally besting Europe's No 1

indicators.note: with its start taken off, the first letter goes

parts.note: 9th written out is NINTH

indicators.note: besting means beating and replacing, so one letter takes the other's place

parts.note: level in a match, EVEN

indicators.note: number one means the first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Europe is E

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter

parts.note: the last letter of Koepka is A

explanation.surface: A golf commentary: Koepka draws level at the ninth and beats Europe's top player.
explanation.walkthrough: INTH, then EVEN with its E replaced by A gives EVAN. Brooks Koepka is an American golfer.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in the van is to be in the vanguard, at the front, ahead of others.

clue.text: After one, be blown away by Bergman when playing his signature feature?

indicators.note: the rest comes after the I

parts.note: I as the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: playing means at play, moving around, so the letters are reordered
blown away means removed, so those letters vanish

explanation.surface: A fan is overwhelmed by Bergman's trademark performance.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove BE from BERGMAN and rearrange RGMAN. The definition: the director Bergman's first name appears on his signature.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingmar Bergman signed his name with this forename, so it is a part of his autograph.

clue.text: Where orders may be of help to stop Turkish leader being jailed

indicators.note: jailed means locked inside, so the leader goes within

parts.note: ABS, anti-lock braking system, helps a car stop
a bey was a Turkish governor or chief

explanation.surface: Orders given to help stop a Turkish leader from imprisonment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Orders' suggests commands; it means religious orders of monks.
explanation.definitionFit: Abbeys house monastic communities, the religious orders of monks or nuns.

clue.text: 6 with Queen overruling a page

indicators.note: overruling means taking control, so the queen supplants the letter

parts.note: 6-down is RISHI, a guru, who is a SAVANT
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: A sage and the Queen override a page of a document.
explanation.walkthrough: 6-down is RISHI, a sage, or SAVANT; ER replaces its first A.
explanation.definitionFit: A page is a boy attendant, a young servant in a noble household.

clue.text: Supply e.g. WI food for one who cared for bairns

indicators.note: read as supple-ly, in a flexible way, so the letters bend into a new order

explanation.surface: An instruction to provide something like Women's Institute food for a childminder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' is read as an adverb from supple. The WI is Britain's Women's Institute; bairns are Scots children.
explanation.definitionFit: A goodwife was the old Scots term for the mistress of a household, who brought up the children.

clue.text: Opportunity to fire new extra hand

indicators.note: to fire is to dismiss, so the letter is sacked from the word

parts.note: a window is an opportunity, as in a window of opportunity

explanation.surface: A chance to sack a new temporary worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' and 'hand' suggest employment; hand means cards dealt.
explanation.definitionFit: In some card games the widow is a spare set of cards dealt face down, an additional hand.

clue.text: Vedette winning gong eventually — entertaining English actress (old-school)

indicators.note: winning a prize means taking it in, so the letter is held inside
entertaining guests means taking them in, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: a vedette is a leading performer, a STAR

indicators.note: eventually points to the final letter

parts.note: the last letter of gong is G

explanation.surface: A star eventually wins an award and hosts an old-fashioned English actress.
explanation.walkthrough: STAR takes in G to give STAGR, which then takes in E.
explanation.definitionFit: Stager is an old term for a theatrical performer, surviving mainly in 'old stager'.

clue.text: Two gallons is drinking record for Swede's Xmas booze

indicators.note: drinking means taking in, so the record goes inside

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for gallon, so two give GG
a log is a written record

explanation.surface: Two gallons drunk in one go sets a record for a Swede's Christmas tipple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drinking' fits the booze theme but is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Glogg is mulled wine with spices, a traditional Scandinavian Christmas drink.

clue.text: Steamship docks in port over here!

indicators.note: docking in means coming inside, so these letters go within

explanation.surface: A steamship berths in harbour and someone calls attention.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation is a definition by example: the sound you make to get someone to come over.
explanation.definitionFit: The interjection is a hushed attempt to catch someone's attention, like calling them over.

clue.text: Measure of compensation from Blitz in area close to Ilford

indicators.note: the war sits inside the other two letters
the close of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the last letter of Ilford is D
the Blitz was a bombing campaign in the Second World War

explanation.surface: Compensation for Blitz damage in a district near Ilford, in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: WAR inside A and D. Ilford is a district of east London.
explanation.definitionFit: An award is a sum of damages granted by a court or tribunal as compensation.

clue.text: Some French Lilith, a victim of uxoricide?

parts.note: des is French for some
Lilith is a female demon of Jewish folklore

explanation.surface: A French reference to Lilith, cast as a murdered wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Uxoricide is the killing of a wife by her husband; Othello smothers his wife in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.definitionFit: Desdemona is the wife strangled by her jealous husband Othello in Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: 50 men & women, 20+ birds and some bling is what you will have been sent by then

definitions.text: 50 men & women, 20+ birds and some bling is what you will have been sent by then

parts.words: 50 men & women, 20+ birds and some bling is what you will have been sent by then
parts.note: a tally of gifts from the Twelve Days of Christmas carol (lords, ladies, pipers, geese, swans, gold rings), with 'What You Will' as the play's subtitle

explanation.walkthrough: The carol's true love sends drummers, pipers, lords, ladies and milkmaids, many birds and five gold rings; all have arrived by the last day. Shakespeare's comedy is subtitled 'What You Will'.
explanation.definitionFit: The evening of 5 January ends the Christmas season, the final day of the carol's gift-giving.
